opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's evolved quite a bit, honestly.

When we started, I think the instinct, coming from machine learning, was to treat it as a modeling problem: build a really good generative model of materials, add a strong property predictor, and you're most of the way there. Over time I've come to see that the model is only one piece. The real challenge is the whole loop.

First, the search space is enormous, and most of it is irrelevant. So you need generative models that respect physics and chemistry: symmetries, stability, synthesizability. Equivariance and those inductive biases matter a lot when data is scarce, and in materials data is almost always scarce.

Second, you can't trust any single predictor. So the design shifted toward a layered approach. Fast, cheap ML surrogates screen enormous numbers of candidates. More expensive simulation, like DFT or molecular dynamics, checks the promising ones. And then, eventually, real experiments. Uncertainty becomes central, because the system has to know when it doesn't know and decide where to spend the expensive compute or lab time. That's essentially active learning, or Bayesian experimental design, at the platform level.

Third, and this was maybe the biggest shift for me, the bottleneck is often the problem definition, not the algorithm. A customer says "I want a better sorbent for carbon capture," but what they actually need involves cost, stability under humidity, manufacturability, and toxicity. So a lot of the design work goes into multi-objective formulation and into making the system something domain scientists can steer, rather than an oracle that just spits out answers.

So I'd say I moved from thinking about "a model for materials" to thinking about an operating system for discovery. It combines generation, simulation, uncertainty, and human expertise, all tied together in a closed loop that gets smarter with every iteration. And of course the motivation underneath it all is climate. If we can shorten the time to find new materials for carbon capture, batteries, or catalysts from decades to years, that's one of the most impactful things AI can do.

r001.rationale: The response says the design “evolved quite a bit” and describes a shift from a model-focused approach to a closed-loop discovery platform, contradicting the claim that it remained largely unchanged.

r002.rationale: It describes generative models alongside simulations, but does not characterize the platform as combining a candidate-generating model with a digital twin.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's evolved quite a lot, honestly. When we started CuspAI, the mental model I had was still very much the physicist's model: you have a target property, you build a generative model over molecular or crystal structures, you condition on the property, and out come candidates. Very clean, very end-to-end. And that picture isn't wrong, but it turned out to be maybe twenty percent of the actual problem.

The first thing that changed was realizing that the generative model is not the bottleneck. We can generate enormous numbers of plausible structures. The bottleneck is knowing which of them you should actually believe in, and whether anyone can make them. So a lot of our thinking shifted from "generate" to "verify and prioritize." That means investing heavily in the simulation stack, in machine-learned force fields and surrogates for DFT that are fast enough to screen at scale but calibrated enough that we know when to distrust them. Uncertainty quantification went from being a nice academic topic to being the thing that determines whether the whole loop works.

The second shift was about synthesizability and the lab. Early on I think I underestimated how much the physical world pushes back. A structure can be thermodynamically beautiful and still be unmakeable with any reasonable synthesis route, or it degrades in humidity, or the precursors cost a fortune. So we moved toward designing the platform as a closed loop with experiment in it from the beginning, rather than treating the lab as the final exam you take after the computation is done. The wet lab is a data source that should feed back into the models, and the models should be choosing experiments that are maximally informative, not just maximally promising. That's active learning in the classical sense, but doing it for real with chemists in the loop is a very different engineering problem than doing it in a Jupyter notebook.

The third thing, which I find intellectually the most interesting, is the role of physical inductive bias versus scale. My whole research program for a decade was about building symmetry into networks, equivariance and so on. And I still believe those priors matter enormously in the data-poor regime, which is exactly where materials live. But I've become more pragmatic. Sometimes a big model with a lot of simulation data and modest inductive bias simply wins, and you have to be honest about that. So now I think of equivariance less as a dogma and more as one knob among several. Where do you spend your bits: on the architecture, on the data, or on the physics simulator that generates the data? That tradeoff is really the design question of the whole platform.

And finally, there's a cultural dimension I didn't appreciate. Building a company around this means you have to pick a target where the error bars of the science and the timelines of the business overlap. Carbon capture materials were a deliberate choice partly for that reason. The problem is important, the property space is well defined, and you can get experimental feedback in weeks rather than years. If I'd designed the platform purely as a general-purpose materials engine, we'd have had a lovely demo and no way to know if it was working.

r001.rationale: The response says the design evolved substantially, shifting from candidate generation toward verification, prioritization, and experimental feedback.

r002.rationale: It describes a generative model and simulation tools, but does not characterize the platform as combining candidate generation with a digital twin.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest shift is from thinking about it as a prediction problem to thinking about it as a discovery loop. You can build a model that predicts a material’s properties, but that alone doesn’t tell you which material to make next, whether you can actually synthesize it, or what you should do when the experiment disagrees with the prediction.

So I would put much more emphasis on connecting those pieces. You propose a candidate, you evaluate it with simulations or experiments, and you use that feedback to decide where to look next. Uncertainty becomes very important there. Sometimes the most useful experiment is one that teaches you something, rather than one that simply tests your highest-scoring candidate.

And that changes how you think about the platform. The model is one component. The real question is whether the whole system helps scientists make better decisions and learn faster.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a major shift from prediction to a discovery loop, not a design that remained largely unchanged.

r002.rationale: It mentions proposing candidates and evaluating them with simulations or experiments, but does not describe the platform as combining a candidate-generating model with a digital twin.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d frame the evolution as moving from thinking about a model to thinking about the whole discovery loop. A model can propose a material with very attractive predicted properties, but that’s only useful if you can make it, measure it, and learn from the result.

So the platform needs to connect those pieces: generating candidates, evaluating them, deciding which experiment is most informative, and feeding the measurements back into the model. Uncertainty matters a great deal here. You want to distinguish between a candidate that looks promising because you have good evidence and one that looks promising because the model is extrapolating.

And the objective is rarely just one property. You also care about stability, synthesis, cost. That pushes the design toward a system where scientists can express those constraints and steer the search. The interesting question becomes: how do we make each experiment improve our ability to choose the next one?

r001.rationale: The response describes an evolution from focusing on a model to designing the whole discovery loop, rather than saying the platform’s design remained largely unchanged.

r002.rationale: It describes candidate generation, evaluation, experiments, and feedback, but does not identify or clearly describe a digital twin.
